outcome: No proof, disproof, or bound movement on the original (first) Euclid–Mullin sequence's every-prime question was found since 26 January 2024; a February 2026 paper by Booker and Simon explicitly reaffirms that both of Mullin's original questions about the first sequence remain open with little known, while the substantive results found (Booker 2013 on the second sequence, a 2016 variant construction) either predate the window or concern a different (related, not the stated) sequence.
summary: The question is whether every prime appears in the (first) Euclid–Mullin sequence (2, 3, 7, 43, 13, 53, 5, ...), defined by taking the smallest prime factor of one plus the product of all previous terms. This remains completely open. The most recent substantive paper touching this family, Booker and Simon's 'A generalisation of the Euclid–Mullin sequences' (arXiv:2601.21901, submitted 2 February 2026), studies cyclotomic-polynomial analogues of Mullin's *second* sequence (largest-prime-factor variant, generalised to residue classes) and proves, under ERH and unconditionally for several moduli, that these analogues omit infinitely many primes. Crucially, the paper's own text states 'As for the first sequence, both of Mullin's questions remain open, and very little is known' — i.e. the authors themselves confirm no progress on the problem as stated in this bullet. Andrew Booker's earlier resolution of the Cox–van der Poorten conjecture (that the *second* Euclid–Mullin sequence omits infinitely many primes) dates to 2011/2013, well before the window, and in any case concerns the second sequence, a related-but-different problem (built with 'largest prime factor' instead of 'smallest prime factor'), not a case of the first sequence. A 2016 paper (arXiv:1605.08929) exhibiting a variant Euclid sequence that provably contains every prime is likewise a different construction ('a' variant, not 'the' Euclid–Mullin sequence) and also predates the window. No computational extension of the known sequence (e.g. resolving whether 41, 47, 67, 73, 79, 83 ever appear) was found past the 2012-era Pollack/Treviño account, which is itself pre-window and in any case would only be a 'found one more term' result, not a settlement of the infinitude-style question per §3.1. No AI system was found anywhere near this problem; the search for AI-related mathematical work near Euclid–Mullin turned up only an unrelated KNAW seminar abstract about deep learning and proofs in general, with no connection to this sequence. The triage's 'none' verdict is upheld.
competing_reading: None of substance. One could argue the Booker–Simon 2026 paper is 'about' the Euclid–Mullin family broadly and thus worth a 'progress' status, but by §3.1 a result about the second sequence's residue-class analogues is a related problem (a changed question: different selection rule, different target set), not a restriction of the first sequence's stated question, so it does not count as progress on this bullet.
what_would_settle_it: Any of: a proof or disproof that every prime appears in the first Euclid–Mullin sequence; a proof that some specific prime (e.g. 41) can never appear; or an explicit authoritative statement updating the list of primes with unknown status in the first sequence, dated after 26 January 2024.
